text: Choose what needs its own controls
After this you can select important configuration items and explain the selection.

Not every part needs its own approval history. A configuration item is a hardware or software element selected for distinct tracking and change control. Choose it because its behavior, interfaces, safety implications, replacement needs or support history make an independent record worthwhile. Selection is a trade-off: too few items hide significant changes, while too many create records nobody can maintain. Write down the boundary and why it matters.

items: List candidate assemblies or software components. You should see: Candidates come from the product map. If not: Return to the product boundary if a major group is missing.
Assess effects of an uncontrolled alteration. You should see: You can explain the consequence in ordinary terms. If not: Consider interfaces, maintenance and operation.
Decide which elements merit independent approval and history. You should see: Each chosen item has an explicit reason. If not: Combine low-risk pieces if separate control adds no value.
Assign a responsible owner and record the decision. You should see: The item can be traced over time. If not: Do not create an orphan item with no owner.
Control software may need separate tracking. Its version can change independently and affect operations. A decorative case cap may not.

text: Give independent control where an independent change could matter.
A tiny item can still be critical when it affects safety or compatibility.

items: Selecting parts only by price Low-cost components can control essential behavior. Fix: Use consequence, interface and support criteria too.
